Record date: 2130-02-06
South Elizabeth Seychelles Hospital INTERNAL MEDICINE DEPARTMENT Location: 4923 Olivia Parkway Suite 217, Lake Jennabury
PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 02/06/30 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Persistent shortness of breath and increased sputum production with ongoing fatigue.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for a follow-up visit after 48 hours of continued Piperacillin-tazobactam therapy. The patient reports no significant change in his respiratory status, stating that he continues to experience shortness of breath, particularly during exertion, and an increase in the volume of yellow-green sputum. He describes the sputum as thicker and more tenacious compared to the previous visit. Fatigue remains a prominent issue, impacting his daily activities, and he reports feeling more fatigued than before.
He denies any new fevers but mentions that he continues to experience intermittent low-grade fevers. Mr. Fairfax has been compliant with his medication regimen, including the increased supplemental oxygen, but he expresses concern over his ongoing symptoms. He has been utilizing his nebulizer as prescribed, although he notes that the relief is temporary.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + persistent fatigue, - night sweats, - chills, + intermittent low-grade fever. Pulmonary - + productive cough with thick yellow-green sputum, + dyspnea, + wheezing, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, - orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - + mild epigastric discomfort, - stable heartburn, - nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - no joint pain. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 128/80 mmHg - Heart Rate: 90 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 28 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 80% on supplemental oxygen (20 L via nasal cannula).
General: The patient appears fatigued and is in moderate respiratory distress, requiring assistance with positioning.
HEENT: No nasal flaring; oropharynx clear, no signs of dehydration.
Lungs: Severe wheezing on auscultation; diminished breath sounds bilaterally; prolonged expiration with rhonchi; crackles noted throughout lung fields, especially in the lower lobes.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs or gallops; peripheral pulses intact.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender; mild epigastric discomfort noted; no hepatosplenomegaly.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation with significant bacterial infection, likely persistent Pseudomonas aeruginosa; sputum characteristics raise concern for inadequate response to current antibiotic therapy. 2. Ongoing respiratory distress with inadequate improvement despite antibiotic treatment; the thickening of sputum is indicative of possible bronchial obstruction or ongoing infection. 3. Persistent fatigue impacting quality of life; gastrointestinal symptoms remain stable.
PLAN
1. Transition antibiotic therapy to Meropenem 1 g every 8 hours intravenously, given the lack of improvement with Piperacillin-tazobactam; reassess after 48 hours and adjust based on clinical response and culture results. 2. Continue oral Prednisone at 60 mg daily, with a tapering plan contingent upon clinical improvement; maintain Omeprazole at 40 mg daily to prevent gastrointestinal side effects. 3. Increase supplemental oxygen to 25 L via nasal cannula; closely monitor for any signs of respiratory distress or hypoxemia. 4. Schedule a repeat chest X-ray to evaluate for any new complications, such as pneumonia or pleural effusion; consider bronchoscopy for further evaluation if no significant improvement is noted. 5. Continue nebulized bronchodilator therapy (Albuterol) every four hours as needed, and maintain Ipratropium bromide therapy; consider adding a mucolytic agent to assist with sputum clearance. 6. Schedule follow-up visit in 48 hours to reassess respiratory function, sputum characteristics, and overall clinical condition; consider referral to pulmonology if no significant improvement is observed.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax will remain under close observation in the internal medicine unit. The treatment team will continue to monitor his clinical status, particularly focusing on respiratory function and infection management. Patient education will be reinforced regarding the importance of adherence to the treatment regimen and the need to report any new or worsening symptoms, particularly related to respiratory function or changes in sputum production.
